purpose.question: How far has the melting front moved after one hour, and does the energy that enters through the wall equal the latent heat plus the sensible heat?

variables.meaning: Density of both phases (the density of ice; the model neglects the change at melting)
Specific heat capacity of water at 0 °C
Specific heat capacity of ice at 0 °C
Specific latent heat of melting of ice
Superheat of the wall above the melting temperature
Subcooling of the ice below the melting temperature
Time of the question: one hour
Far end of the solid, far beyond the thermal layer (the model takes it to infinity)
Front position at the time of the question

geometry.domain: A half-space of ice x > 0 behind a plane wall at x = 0; water fills 0 < x < s(t)
geometry.coordinates: x from the wall into the ice, and time t
geometry.interfaces: The melting front x = s(t)

assumptions.text: Constant properties in each phase. Conduction only: the water does not move.
Both phases have the density of ice. Water at 0 °C is 9 % denser (999.8 kg/m³); the model neglects the flow that the change of density causes.
The front is sharp and at the melting temperature: no supercooling and no mushy zone.
The solid is a half-space: x_f is far beyond the thermal layer, and the similarity solution takes x_f → ∞.
Properties of water at 0.01 °C and of ice at 0 °C from Lienhard and Lienhard, Tables A.2 and A.3; latent heat 333.3 kJ/kg (Problem 5.31).

scales.reason: The diffusion length (α_l t_r)^(1/2) of the liquid at the time of the question.
The same length for the front.
The time of the question.
θ_l = 1 at the wall and 0 at the front.
θ_s = 0 at the front and −1 in the undisturbed ice.

evidence.claim: The two-phase Neumann solution: erf profiles in each phase, s = 2λ(α_l t)^(1/2) and the transcendental equation for λ (eqs. 3.28 to 3.31 with fractional order 1).

quantities.about: The quantity vocabulary of the variable table. A variable may name one quantity; its dimension must agree with the unit and the dimension formula. Familiar groups (groups.json) match on these ids, never on symbols. temperature: absolute or difference. meaning: the physical meaning a dimensionless quantity keeps.

quantities.name: thermal contact resistance per unit area
bending stiffness of a plate or shell
empirical surface constant of a correlation
emissive power or intensity times π

groups.about: Familiar dimensionless groups, each stored as formulas over quantities with explicit reference quantities, never as a name alone (spec section 10). A group matches a calculated group when one of its forms gives the same exponent for each supplied variable through a one-to-one match of quantities. phase, kind and role narrow a term: phase fluid or solid; kind parameter (the default, which also matches a constant), field, coordinate or any. A recognized name is a proposed interpretation until the researcher confirms it. Order is the preference order for a familiar basis.

groups.label: Nu
groups.name: Nusselt number
groups.reference: L is the characteristic length of the declared geometry and k_f is the fluid conductivity. State whether h and Nu are local or mean values.

groups.label: λ²
groups.name: fin parameter squared, with λ = mL
groups.reference: L is the fin length, P the exposed perimeter and A_c the cross-sectional area.

groups.label: Q̇L/(kA_cΔT)
groups.name: base heat flow in dimensionless form
groups.reference: ΔT = T_b − T_∞ is the base excess temperature and must not be 0.

groups.label: PL/A_c
groups.name: ratio of perimeter times length to cross-sectional area
groups.reference: A geometry ratio of the fin.

groups.label: A_c/L²
groups.name: ratio of cross-sectional area to length squared
groups.reference: A geometry ratio of the fin.

groups.label: Bi
groups.name: Biot number
groups.reference: Bi needs the Biot length L_c and the solid conductivity k_s. L_c = V/A_s is the half-thickness of a slab cooled on both faces, r/2 for a long cylinder and r/3 for a sphere. A spatial solution uses the half-thickness or the radius.

groups.label: θ
groups.name: normalized temperature
groups.reference: The two differences must share one reference temperature, such as T_∞. The reference difference must not be 0.

groups.label: X
groups.name: dimensionless position
groups.reference: x is the coordinate and L the length scale of the declared domain, such as the half-thickness.

groups.label: Fo
groups.name: Fourier number
groups.reference: α_s is the solid diffusivity and L_c the same length as in Bi. When t is the time coordinate, Fo is the dimensionless time.

groups.label: Re
groups.name: Reynolds number
groups.reference: U is the reference speed and L the characteristic length. Use the same L as in Nu when an identity combines them.

groups.label: Pr
groups.name: Prandtl number
groups.reference: Pr is a ratio of fluid properties. Take all properties at one reference temperature.

groups.label: Pe
groups.name: Péclet number
groups.reference: Pe = Re Pr only when Re and Pr use the same reference properties.

groups.label: St_h
groups.name: Stanton number
groups.reference: State whether h and St_h are local or mean values.

groups.label: Gr
groups.name: Grashof number
groups.reference: State whether ΔT is a positive scale or a signed difference.

groups.label: Ra
groups.name: Rayleigh number
groups.reference: Ra = Gr Pr only when both use the same reference properties.

groups.label: Ri
groups.name: bulk Richardson number
groups.reference: A bulk Richardson number. The gradient Richardson number is a different quantity.

groups.label: Ste
groups.name: Stefan number
groups.reference: State the phase of c_p and the temperature interval of ΔT.

groups.label: Ec
groups.name: Eckert number
groups.reference: ΔT is a positive scale.

groups.label: Br
groups.name: Brinkman number
groups.reference: Br = Pr Ec only when both use the same reference properties.

groups.label: Ma_T
groups.name: thermal Marangoni number
groups.reference: Ma_T is a positive magnitude. Keep the sign of dγ/dT separately.

groups.label: NTU
groups.name: number of transfer units
groups.reference: U_HX is the overall heat-transfer coefficient, not a speed.

groups.label: C_r
groups.name: capacity rate ratio
groups.reference: C = ṁ c_p for each stream.

groups.label: τ_opt
groups.name: optical thickness
groups.reference: κ_a is the absorption coefficient of the medium.

sources.supports: The separation-of-variables solution for transient conduction in a slab (plane wall) with convection at the surfaces (Newton's law of cooling) and a symmetry condition at the centre line, as functions of the Biot and Fourier numbers. The page says that the solutions for the infinite cylinder and the sphere are "even messier" and that its workbook solves their characteristic equations.

They are however independent and form a complete set." It also asks "can I vary all of these variables independently", and it says "Compare with experimental data!"

sources.title: COMSOL 6.3 Heat Transfer Module: Defining the Heat Transfer Coefficients
sources.supports: Nu_L = hL/k, Re_L = ρUL/μ, Pr = μC_p/k, Ra_L = Gr_L Pr, with L the characteristic length.

sources.title: MIT 16 Unified Engineering, thermodynamics notes, section 18.2: Heat Transfer From a Fin
sources.supports: m²L² = hPL²/(kA), the insulated-tip profile cosh(mL(1 − ξ))/cosh(mL) and the base heat flow Q̇/(√(kAhP)(T₀ − T∞)) = tanh(mL).

sources.title: MathJax documentation: MathJax Font Support

sources.title: Specification 6, section 14: verification and completion
sources.supports: The checks before automatic support: residuals for base states, modes and branches, continuation and discretization convergence, and explicit error measures with tolerances.

sources.title: Wen, Goluskin and Doering (2022): Steady Rayleigh–Bénard convection between no-slip boundaries, J. Fluid Mech. 933, R4, with its supplementary material
sources.supports: No-slip isothermal plates with the conductive state (u, T) = (0, 1 − z). Onset at Ra_c ≈ 1708, where a roll pair of period Γ ≈ 2.016 bifurcates supercritically. Nu = 1 + (Pr Ra)^{1/2}⟨wT⟩. Table 1S of the supplementary material gives Nu and Re of steady rolls at Pr = 1 and Γ = 2.

sources.title: Lienhard IV and Lienhard V: A Heat Transfer Textbook, 6th edition, version 6.00 (19 April 2024)
sources.supports: The lumped model is accurate within about 3 % if Bi < 0.1 (section 1.3). The radiation coefficient h_rad = 4σT_m³ε needs (ΔT/T_m)²/4 ≪ 1 (equations 2.28 to 2.31). View factor reciprocity and summation, the string rule (problem 10.14) and radiosity networks of grey surfaces (section 10.4). Properties of water at 300 K (Table A.3) and of pure copper (Table A.1). Piece 7: the laminar flat-plate correlations Nu_x = 0.332 Re_x^(1/2) Pr^(1/3) for Pr ≥ 0.6, within 2 % of the exact solution (eqn. 6.58), and Nu_L = 0.664 Re_L^(1/2) Pr^(1/3) (eqn. 6.68); the turbulent gas correlation 0.0296 Re_x^0.8 Pr^0.6 (eqn. 6.112); the transition data of section 6.1; the Péclet number (eqn. 6.61); Churchill and Chu's eqns. (8.13a) and (8.13b) with Example 8.1; inclined walls with g cos θ (section 8.4); and Gr/Re² for mixed convection with assisting and opposing flow (eqn. 8.45). Piece 8: the effectiveness ε = Q/(C_min(T_h,in − T_c,in)), NTU = UA/C_min and the parallel-flow and counterflow relations (eqns. 3.16 to 3.21), the single-stream limit (3.22), the balanced limit NTU/(1 + NTU) (3.23) with Examples 3.2 and 3.5; water at 0.01 °C and ice at 0 °C (Tables A.2 and A.3) and h_sf = 333.3 kJ/kg (Problem 5.31); Nusselt's film (eqns. 8.46 to 8.62), the film Reynolds number and its limits 7 and 400 (eqn. 8.72, Fig. 8.15) and Example 8.6; Rohsenow's correlation (9.4) with Table 9.2, its data from 1 atm to 167.7 atm (Fig. 9.7) and typical errors of 100 % in q and 25 % in ΔT, the Taylor wavelength (9.6a), the peak heat flux (9.11) with its conditions, the Zuber–Kutateladze value (9.12), and Examples 9.2 and 9.5.

sources.title: NIST CODATA 2018: Stefan–Boltzmann constant
sources.supports: σ = 5.670 374 419… × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, exact in the SI. The page uses its first 10 digits.

sources.title: Farrell, Beentjes and Birkisson: The computation of disconnected bifurcation diagrams (arXiv:1603.00809)
sources.supports: Continuation from known solutions finds only the branches connected to them. Disconnected branches need a separate method, such as deflation. A branch search has a stated coverage, not a guarantee of completeness.

sources.title: MIT 16.01 Unified Engineering (2004): Key concepts for materials and structures, handout for the spring quizzes
sources.supports: The Euler load of a perfect pinned column, P_E = π²EI/L², buckling into a half sine wave (page 4). The midspan deflection 5q₀L⁴/(384EI) of a simply supported beam under a uniform load (page 2).

sources.title: Holmes: Elasticity and stability of shape-changing structures (arXiv:1809.04620)
sources.supports: The elastica: λ_p² = P/B, P_c = π²B/L², k = sin(α/2) and Λ(k) = 2mK[k] with m = 1 for mode one. With the arc length scaled to 0 ≤ s ≤ 1 this gives PL²/B = 4K(k)²; that last step is the page's own.

sources.title: Yong and Mahadevan: Lyapunov–Schmidt bifurcation analysis of a supported compressible elastic beam (arXiv:2501.08028)
sources.supports: The inextensible Euler beam has a supercritical bifurcation at the critical load, but a compressible beam on a foundation can have subcritical pitchforks: the classification depends on the model.

sources.title: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, section 19.5: Maclaurin and related expansions
University of Alberta, Vibrations and Sound: damped spring–mass system under harmonic force
sources.supports: Equation 5.14: X/δ_ST = 1/√([1 − (ω/p)²]² + [2ζω/p]²), with p² = k/m and ζ = c/(2√(mk)) from the free-vibration page (equations 3.5 and 3.6).

sources.title: MIT 16.20 Structural Mechanics (2002), Unit 23: Vibration of continuous systems
sources.supports: A pinned beam has ω_r = r²π²√(EI/(ml⁴)) and the modes sin(rπx/l) (pages 23-9 and 23-10).

sources.title: Kelly: Solid Mechanics Part II, section 6 Plate theory, University of Auckland
sources.supports: Navier's solution: A_mn = 16q/(π⁶Dmn)(m²/a² + n²/b²)⁻² for odd m, n (equation 6.5.50), and w ≈ 0.0040624qa⁴/D at the centre of a square plate (equation 6.5.52).

sources.title: MIT 2.081J Plates and Shells (2007), lecture notes
sources.supports: D = Eh³/(12(1 − ν²)) (page 11). A cylinder under lateral pressure: Dw'''' + Ehw/a² = q, w'''' + 4β⁴w = q/D, a solution that decays as e^(−βx) and a bending zone of the width π/(2β) (section 5.1.2, pages 87 and 88). Equation 387 prints β⁴ = Eh/(a²D) = 3(1 − ν²)/(a²h⁴); from equation 386 the correct form is Eh/(4a²D) = 3(1 − ν²)/(a²h²), which the page uses.

sources.title: Purdue ME 323: Thermal deformations
sources.supports: A free rod expands by αΔTL with no stress; a rod with both ends fixed has P = −EAαΔT and σ = −EαΔT.

sources.title: Hutchinson: Stresses and failure modes in thin films and multilayers, DCAMM course notes (1996)
sources.supports: Equation 2.4: a film held in its plane (ε = 0) under a temperature change has the equal biaxial stress −EαΔT/(1 − ν).

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center: Mass flow choking
sources.supports: The mass flow rate ṁ = (Ap_t/√T_t)√(γ/R) M (1 + (γ − 1)M²/2)^(−(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))) (eq. 10). Its derivative is 0 only at M = 1, the maximum (eqs. 14 to 19). Choking at the throat, the smallest area.

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center: Normal shock wave equations
sources.supports: The static pressure ratio across a normal shock, p₁/p₀ = (2γM² − (γ − 1))/(γ + 1), with M the upstream Mach number.

sources.title: Lienhard IV and Lienhard V: A Heat Transfer Textbook, 6th edition, version 6.00 (19 April 2024), chapters 6 and 7
sources.supports: The Hagen–Poiseuille profile (eqn. 7.14), the laminar friction factor f = 64/Re_D, Nu_D = 48/11 = 4.364 for a uniform wall heat flux (eqn. 7.22), the parallel-plate profile (eqn. 7.62) and Nu_Dh = 8.235 for a fixed flux at both plates (eqn. 7.63). The Blasius solution f''(0) = 0.33206 (Table 6.1) and c_f = 0.664/√Re_x (eqns. 6.32 and 6.33). Piece 7: Nu_D = 3.657 for a uniform wall temperature (eqn. 7.23), the thermal entry lengths 0.034 and 0.043 Re_D Pr (eqn. 7.24), the minimum transitional Re_D ≈ 2100, and Gnielinski's correlation with Filonenko's friction factor for 2300 ≤ Re_D ≤ 5 × 10⁶ and 0.6 ≤ Pr ≤ 10⁵ (eqns. 7.41 and 7.42).

sources.title: Apsley: Hydraulics 3, open-channel flow, rapidly-varied flow (University of Manchester)
sources.supports: The hydraulic jump: sequent depths h₂/h₁ = (√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)/2 from the momentum principle, the head loss (h₂ − h₁)³/(4h₁h₂), and a jump only from supercritical to subcritical flow. The specific energy E = h + q²/(2gh²), its minimum (3/2)h_c at h_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) where Fr = 1, and the alternate depths.

sources.title: Delestre et al.: SWASHES, a compilation of shallow water analytic solutions for hydraulic and environmental studies (arXiv:1110.0288)
sources.supports: The one-dimensional shallow-water equations, the characteristic speeds u ± √(gh), and the boundary data: a subcritical flow needs one upstream and one downstream value, a supercritical flow two upstream values.

sources.title: MIT 16.110: boundary-layer analysis of an aerodynamic flow
sources.supports: Two domains, the viscous shear layer and the outer flow, with the small parameter ε ~ Re^(−1/2). The inner rescaling Y = y/ε and V = v/ε. The viscous terms dropped from the outer flow.

sources.title: MIT 16.01 Unified Engineering, Fluids lecture notes F18: vortex and lifting flow about a circular cylinder
sources.supports: Uniform flow, doublet and vortex give the lifting flow about a circular cylinder. The surface pressure C_p = 1 − (2 sin θ + Γ/(2πV R))², and the forces from the surface pressure integral.

sources.title: MIT 18.354 (Spring 2014), lecture 21: classical aerofoil theory
sources.supports: The Joukowski transformation of a circle into an aerofoil, the circulation that makes the velocity finite at the trailing edge (the Kutta–Joukowski condition), and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem: lift ρu₀Γ and zero drag.

sources.title: MIT 16.01 Unified Engineering, Fluids lecture 4: thin airfoil theory, analysis example
sources.supports: The parabolic-arc camber line z = 4εx(1 − x/c) with slope 4ε cos θ. A₀ = α, A₁ = 4ε, A₂ = 0. C_l = π(2A₀ + A₁) = 2π(α + 2ε) and c_m,c/4 = (π/4)(A₂ − A₁) = −πε.

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center: Inclination effects on lift
sources.supports: For thin airfoils the lift is proportional to the angle of attack for small angles (within ±10°). At higher angles the boundary layer separates and the wing stalls.

sources.title: University of Sydney aerodynamics notes: Flow around a circular cylinder (copy at the University of Cambridge)
sources.supports: Potential flow gives C_p = 1 − 4 sin²θ and zero drag (d'Alembert's paradox). In a real flow viscosity causes separation behind the cylinder, and the agreement with experiment is lost there.

sources.title: COMSOL Multiphysics Cyclopedia: Marangoni effect
sources.supports: The tangential stress at a free surface τ = (∂σ/∂T)(∂T/∂s). The liquid flows toward regions of higher surface tension, so toward the cold side when the surface tension falls with temperature. Ma = |∂σ/∂T|ΔT L/(μα). The flow couples with heat transport.

sources.title: MIT 2.810 Manufacturing Processes and Systems (2016): Quiz 1 solutions, problem 4, Viscous heating
sources.supports: The ratio of the rate of viscous heating to the rate of transverse heat conduction is the Brinkman number Br = μv²/(kΔT). Br > 1 means that viscous heating exceeds the transverse heat loss by conduction.

sources.title: MIT 1.63J/2.21J Advanced Fluid Dynamics of the Environment (Mei, 2002), notes 5.2: Kelvin–Helmholtz instability for continuous shear and stratification
sources.supports: The gradient Richardson number Ri = −(g/ρ)(dρ/dz)/(dU/dz)² (eqn. 5.2.1), a local ratio of the vertical density gradient to the square of the vertical shear, and the Miles–Howard result that instability needs Ri < 1/4.

sources.title: Bannerman: Heat, Mass and Momentum Transfer, Heat Exchanger Notes (University of Aberdeen)
sources.supports: The heat-transfer effectiveness ε = Q/Q_max with Q_max = C_min(T_h,in − T_c,in), NTU = UA/C_min and c = C_min/C_max (eqs. 23 to 27), and that ε depends on NTU and c for each flow arrangement. Its table of effectiveness relations is an image; the page takes the relations from Lienhard and Lienhard, eqs. (3.20) and (3.21).

sources.title: Font: A one-phase Stefan problem with size-dependent thermal conductivity (preprint, UPC Barcelona, 2018)
sources.supports: The one-phase Stefan problem (eqs. 2 to 5), its Neumann solution s = 2λt^(1/2) with βπ^(1/2)λ erf(λ)e^(λ²) = 1 (eqs. 7 and 8), the Stefan number written as β = ΔH/(ρc(T_f − T_c)) (the reciprocal of the page's Ste), and a boundary-immobilization (front-fixing) finite-difference scheme (section 4).

sources.title: Roscani and Tarzia: A generalized Neumann solution for the two-phase fractional Lamé–Clapeyron–Stefan problem (arXiv:1405.5928)
sources.supports: With fractional order 1, the classical two-phase Stefan problem of a half-space with one density (eq. 3.32), the erf and erfc temperatures of each phase, s = 2μλ₁t^(1/2) and the transcendental equation for the coefficient (eqs. 3.28 to 3.31).

sources.title: Beach, Özişik and Siewert: Radiative transfer in linearly anisotropic-scattering, conservative and non-conservative slabs with reflective boundaries, Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer 14 (1971) 1551–1565
sources.supports: Table 1: the heat-flux functions Q_0(0), Q_1(0) and Q_1*(τ_0) of an absorbing, emitting medium at constant temperature between black and grey walls at τ_0 = 0.1, 1 and 10; for c = 0 and black walls these are 1 − 2E_3(τ_0) and 2E_3(τ_0).

sources.title: COMSOL 6.4 Heat Transfer Module: Radiation in participating media, the Rosseland approximation
sources.supports: The Rosseland approximation q_r = −k_R∇T with k_R = 16n²σT³/(3β_R) holds when the medium is optically thick, τ ≫ 1, and should be validated.

catalogue.about: The declared model catalogue of spec section 10, one entry for each declared model of the families built so far. Each entry has the six parts that section 10 requires: model (equations, closures, geometry, conditions and the declared dimensionless form), domain (parameters and assumptions), operations (symbolic and numerical), methods (the four analyses, each with the reason it applies or not) with limitations, acceptance (standard example, reference and tolerance) and solver (method, discretization, convergence and reproducibility). A record names its declared model in purpose.declaration; the page checks the Nondimensionalizer's result against the declared dimensionless form exactly.

declarations.title: Lumped body with convection

model.summary: A body whose temperature stays uniform, with heat capacity ρc_pV, cooled through its surface A_s by convection to a fluid at T_∞.

roles.meaning: conductivity of the body, for the Biot number

closures: Newton's law of cooling with constant h: the heat flow out of the surface is hA_s(T − T_∞).
model.geometry: Any shape. The Biot length is L_c = V/A_s. The comparison with a spatial model uses the shape in the record's geometry: a slab, a long cylinder, a sphere or a cube (the product of three slab solutions).

assumptions.text: The temperature is uniform in the body at each time. The comparison with the spatial model tests this assumption.
ρ, c_p, h and T_∞ are constant.
T_i is not equal to T_∞.

symbolic: Exact check that the Nondimensionalizer gives θ_τ = −θ and θ(0) = 1 with τ = t/(ρc_pV/(hA_s)).
The exact solution θ = e^{−τ}, checked in canonical form: ∂_τ e^{−τ} + e^{−τ} = 0.
The lumped model as the leading order of the small-Bi expansion of the spatial model (src/asymptotic.js).
numerical: The error of the lumped model against the spatial model of the declared shape, at each point of the map.
The decay time ρc_pV/(hA_s) and the temperature at the record's time.

dominant-balance.reason: The uniform-temperature assumption is a balance: the internal temperature drop is small compared with the drop across the surface film when Bi_c is small.

asymptotic.reason: The lumped model is the leading order of the outer expansion of the spatial model as Bi → 0 with the slow time fixed: a coupled limit.

stability.reason: The model is linear with one steady state θ = 0, and θ = e^{−τ} decays. A stability analysis adds nothing.

bifurcation.reason: The model is linear, so no branch can split.

limitations: The spatial comparison covers a slab, a long cylinder, a sphere and a cube. Other shapes need a separate declaration of the spatial model.
Radiation exchange makes the model nonlinear: piece 4 declares the lumped body with radiation.

acceptance.reference: θ = e^{−τ} (exact) and the decay time ρc_pV/(hA_s) from the record's values (exact). Also the lumped error against the page's slab series at Bi = 0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001 with Bi·Fo = 1.
acceptance.tolerance: Exact for the decay time and the solution. The lumped error must fall with Bi and be below 1e-3 at Bi = 10⁻⁴.
checks: The Nondimensionalizer's equation and condition equal the declared dimensionless model (exact).
The decay time from the record's values is exact, and θ = e^{−τ} solves θ_τ = −θ with θ(0) = 1 (exact).
The lumped error against the spatial model goes to 0 as Bi_c goes to 0 at a fixed Bi_c·Fo_c.

solver.method: Closed form θ = e^{−τ}. The spatial comparison uses the series of the declared shape (transient conduction declarations).
solver.discretization: None for the lumped model. The comparison uses 21 points in X for the slab, the cylinder and the sphere, and 21 × 21 × 21 points in an octant of the cube.
solver.convergence: The same mode count rule as the transient conduction declarations: λ_n²τ ≤ 50.
solver.reproducibility: Plain JavaScript in double precision. Exact rationals for the decay time.

declarations.title: Transient conduction in a slab with surface convection

model.summary: A slab of half-thickness L with constant properties, uniform initial temperature T_i and convection to a fluid at T_∞ on its surface.
closures: The equation contains Fourier's law with constant k: q = −k ∂T/∂x.
model.geometry: A slab of half-thickness L, symmetric about its centre plane x = 0. Both faces see the same fluid.

declarations.title: Boussinesq layer in a box heated from below

model.summary: A two-dimensional cell of depth H and width L lies between no-slip isothermal plates at T_h (below) and T_c (above). It has stress-free adiabatic side walls and follows the Boussinesq approximation. The stream function ψ and the vorticity ω describe the flow. The box holds exactly the mirror-symmetric rolls of a periodic layer of period 2L.

equations.text: d(omega,t) + d(psi,z)*d(omega,x) - d(psi,x)*d(omega,z) = nu*(d(omega,x,x) + d(omega,z,z)) - g*beta*d(T,x)

closures: Boussinesq: the density changes only in the buoyancy term, ρ = ρ_0[1 − β(T − T_c)].
Newtonian viscosity and Fourier conduction with constant ν and κ.
u = ∂ψ/∂z, w = −∂ψ/∂x, so the flow is incompressible.
model.geometry: A two-dimensional cell 0 < x < L, 0 < z < H. Γ = L/H. The plates are horizontal. Gravity points down, in the direction −z.

conditions.meaning: no flow through the lower plate
no slip at the lower plate
no flow through the upper plate
no slip at the upper plate
no flow through the left wall
no shear stress at the left wall
no flow through the right wall
no shear stress at the right wall

equations.text: d(Omega,tau) + d(Psi,Z)*d(Omega,X) - d(Psi,X)*d(Omega,Z) = Pr*(d(Omega,X,X) + d(Omega,Z,Z)) - Pr*Ra*d(theta,X)

symmetry.text: the reflection X → Γ − X with Ψ → −Ψ and Ω → −Ω

assumptions.text: The Boussinesq approximation applies: βΔT ≪ 1, and the properties are constant.
The flow is two-dimensional. With stress-free adiabatic side walls, the box holds exactly the mirror-symmetric rolls of a periodic layer of period 2L.
The plates are no-slip and isothermal, as in Wen, Goluskin and Doering (2022).

symbolic: Exact check that the Nondimensionalizer gives the declared equations and the 14 conditions.
Exact check of the conductive base state θ = 1 − Z, Ψ = Ω = 0 in every equation and condition.
Exact perturbation equations: the order-ε part of the substitution.
Exact check of the reflection symmetry X → Γ − X, Ψ → −Ψ, Ω → −Ω.
numerical: Growth rates σ of each box mode a = nπ/Γ, with the eigenmode and its residual.
The neutral curve Ra(a) of the unbounded layer and its minimum (Ra_c, a_c).
The steady roll branch by Newton's method and continuation in Ra, with Nu, Re and a resolution check.
The amplitude equation at onset, and the stability of the rolls to disturbances of the same period and symmetry.

dominant-balance.reason: At onset, viscous diffusion balances the buoyancy torque. The advection terms are of second order in the amplitude.

asymptotic.reason: The weakly nonlinear expansion in ε = Ra/Ra_c − 1 gives the amplitude equation of the rolls.

stability.reason: The conductive state is a steady solution. Convection starts where the conductive state becomes linearly unstable in time.

bifurcation.reason: Rolls branch from the conductive state at onset. Continuation follows the branch, and the amplitude equation classifies the pitchfork.

limitations: Two-dimensional states in the box only. Three-dimensional convection, turbulence and the cavity heated from the side need separate declarations.
Stress-free adiabatic side walls are an idealization. With rigid side walls the onset is at a higher Ra.
The acceptance test validates the roll branch for Ra ≤ 10⁴ against Wen, Goluskin and Doering (2022) at Pr = 1. The page does not compute it above 10⁴.
Stability of the rolls covers disturbances of the same period and mirror symmetry only.

acceptance.reference: Ra_c and a_c of the unbounded layer from the independent SciPy script (tools/stability_references.py), and Ra_c ≈ 1708 with the period 2.016 (Wen, Goluskin and Doering 2022). Nu of steady rolls at Pr = 1 and period 2 from their Table 1S, at 15 values of Ra up to 10⁴.
acceptance.tolerance: 1e-7 relative for Ra_c, 1e-4 for a_c, 1e-4 relative for Nu, 1e-5 relative between two resolutions.
checks: Ra_c converges between 16 and 24 nodes.
Ra_c and a_c agree with the SciPy reference.
At the critical point the largest growth rate is real and 0.
Nu of the roll branch agrees with Table 1S.
Nu at Ra = 10⁴ converges in the resolution.
The amplitude equation gives a supercritical pitchfork.

solver.method: Chebyshev collocation in z on a basis that meets the wall conditions, W = (1 − ξ²)²p and Θ = (1 − ξ²)q, Thus each eigenproblem is standard. Hessenberg QR gives the eigenvalues. The rolls use Fourier modes in x (ψ odd, θ even), Newton's method and continuation in Ra. A Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction of the discrete system gives the stationary amplitude equation.
solver.discretization: 16 interior nodes for the linear analysis and 14 for the map. 8 Fourier modes × 16 nodes for the rolls, with 32 points in x for the products.
solver.convergence: Ra_c to 1e-9 between 16 and 24 nodes. Nu to 1e-5 between 8 × 16 and 10 × 20. Newton stops at a row-scaled residual of 1e-11.
solver.reproducibility: Plain JavaScript in double precision. The reference script pins NumPy and SciPy.

declarations.title: Lumped body with grey radiation to an enclosure

model.summary: A body has a uniform temperature, the heat capacity ρc_pV and the surface A_s with the emissivity ε. It receives the heat Q and exchanges grey radiation with a large enclosure at T_e.

roles.meaning: conductivity of the body, for the radiation Biot number

closures: Grey diffuse exchange of a small body with a large enclosure: the net loss is εσA_s(T⁴ − T_e⁴) (Lienhard, section 10.4).
model.geometry: Any shape that is small compared with the enclosure. The radiation Biot number uses L_c = V/A_s.

parameters.meaning: supplied heat over the enclosure emission

assumptions.text: The temperature is uniform in the body: the radiation Biot number stays below 0.1 (Lienhard, section 1.3).
The surface is grey and diffuse, and the enclosure is large and at a uniform T_e.
Temperatures are absolute.

symbolic: Exact check that the Nondimensionalizer gives θ_τ = q + 1 − θ⁴ and θ(0) = θ_i.
Exact perturbation equation and the exact derivative f′(θ) = −4θ³.
numerical: The equilibrium (1 + q)^{1/4}, the closed-form transient by Brent's method, and a Dormand–Prince check.
The error of the linearized decay and of the emission-only model at each point of the map.

dominant-balance.reason: Emission θ⁴ balances absorption and supply 1 + q. Far above the equilibrium, emission controls the heat loss.

asymptotic.reason: Near the equilibrium a regular expansion in θ_i − θ* gives the linearized decay with h_rad = 4εσT_e³θ*³.

stability.reason: The equilibrium is a steady state. Its eigenvalue −4θ*³ gives linear stability, and the balance decreases strictly, so the equilibrium attracts every start with θ_i > 0.

bifurcation.reason: f(θ) = q + 1 − θ⁴ decreases strictly for θ > 0. Thus the one equilibrium stays stable, and no branch splits.

limitations: Uniform temperature only: a large radiation Biot number needs a spatial model.
A grey diffuse surface and a large isothermal enclosure only. View factors to a finite enclosure need the surface-radiation model.

acceptance.reference: The equilibrium (1 + q)^{1/4} and the closed form τ = G(θ_i) − G(θ), with G(θ) = ln|(θ − a)/(θ + a)|/(4a³) − arctan(θ/a)/(2a³). An mpmath integration checks it (tools/stability_references.py).
acceptance.tolerance: 1e-12 for the equilibrium, 1e-8 for the transient.
checks: The equilibrium satisfies the balance.
The closed form agrees with the Dormand–Prince integration.
The eigenvalue −4θ*³ is negative.

solver.method: Closed form for the transient (Brent's method on G), and the Dormand–Prince 5(4) integrator as a check.
solver.discretization: None for the closed form. The map has 41 × 31 points.
solver.convergence: Brent to 1e-15. Dormand–Prince with rtol 1e-11 and atol 1e-13.
solver.reproducibility: Plain JavaScript in double precision.

declarations.title: Grey absorbing and emitting slab at a uniform temperature between black walls

model.summary: A plane layer of a grey, absorbing and emitting, non-scattering medium with absorption coefficient κ_a, thickness L and a uniform prescribed temperature T_g lies between two black walls at T_1 and T_2. The radiative-transfer equation along a ray with direction cosine μ is solved exactly for the forward (μ > 0) and backward (μ < 0) intensities.

π times the intensity toward x < 0
|cos| of the angle between the ray and the x axis
temperature of wall 2 at x = L
net radiative heat flux into the medium at wall 1

closures: Kirchhoff's law for a grey medium: the emission term is κ_a times the blackbody intensity σT_g⁴/π, and the absorption is κ_a times the intensity. No scattering. The net heat flux is q = 2∫₀¹(i_p − i_m)μ dμ in terms of i = πI, and the angular integrals of e^(−τ/μ) are the exponential integrals E_3 (Beach, Özişik and Siewert, 1971).
model.geometry: A plane layer 0 < x < L, unbounded in y and z, between two parallel black walls.

conditions.meaning: wall 1 is black: it emits σT_1⁴ and reflects nothing

assumptions.text: A grey, non-scattering medium with a uniform and prescribed temperature T_g: the energy equation of the medium is not solved.
Black, diffuse walls at uniform temperatures. All temperatures are absolute temperatures, and the ratios keep the fourth powers.

The Rosseland approximation q = −(16σT³/(3κ_a)) dT/dx needs an optically thick medium, τ ≫ 1 (COMSOL, Rosseland approximation). The page applies it only where its error is within the stated tolerance.

symbolic: The exact groups τ_L, r_1 = T_1/T_g and r_2 = T_2/T_g in rationals; the exact solution of each ray equation, i = σT_g⁴ + (i_wall − σT_g⁴)e^(−κ_a s/μ).
The angular integrals in closed form: the slab emissivity ε_s = 1 − 2E_3(τ_L), the transmissivity 2E_3(τ_L) and the net fluxes at both walls.
numerical: E_n(x) by its series or its continued fraction, to about 1e-15.
An independent check: the net fluxes and the absorbed power from Gauss–Legendre quadrature in μ and x of the exact ray solutions, against the closed form.

dominant-balance.reason: Along a ray, the change of the intensity balances emission minus absorption. τ_L/μ compares the path with the mean free path 1/κ_a. For τ_L ≪ 1 the wall intensities pass almost unchanged (optically thin); for τ_L ≫ 1 the medium emits as a black body at T_g except within a few mean free paths of each wall (optically thick).

asymptotic.reason: Thin limit: ε_s = 2τ_L + O(τ_L² ln τ_L). Thick limit: ε_s = 1 − 2E_3(τ_L), with 2E_3(τ_L) < e^(−τ_L). Rosseland diffusion predicts no net flux inside a uniform medium; the exact flux at the mid-plane is 2E_3(τ_L/2)σ(T_1⁴ − T_2⁴), so the page draws where that error is within the tolerance.

stability.reason: The declared model is linear in the intensities with a prescribed temperature. It has one solution and no dynamics.

bifurcation.reason: Linear model with a unique solution for each τ_L, r_1 and r_2: no branches.

limitations: A prescribed uniform temperature of the medium: radiative equilibrium, or coupling with conduction or convection, needs a separate declaration with the energy equation of the medium.
Grey and non-scattering only; band models of real gases need a separate declaration.
Black walls only; grey walls need the radiosity balance of each wall.

acceptance.reference: Beach, Özişik and Siewert (1971), Table 1, c = 0, black walls (ε_1 = ε_2 = 1): Q_0(0) = 0.1674, 0.7806 and 1.0000 and Q_1*(τ_0) = 0.8326, 0.2194 and 0.0 at τ_0 = 0.1, 1 and 10. These are the slab emissivity 1 − 2E_3(τ_0) and the transmissivity 2E_3(τ_0).

The net fluxes from quadrature of the exact ray solutions equal the closed form.
The power that the medium absorbs equals the difference of the net wall fluxes.

declarations.title: Melting of a half-space: two-phase Stefan model (Neumann)

model.summary: A solid half-space x > 0 starts at the uniform temperature T_i ≤ T_m. At t = 0 the wall x = 0 goes to T_w > T_m, and a liquid layer 0 < x < s(t) grows. Each phase conducts heat with constant properties; both phases have one density; the front x = s(t) is at the melting temperature and moves by the Stefan condition. With T_i = T_m the model is the one-phase Stefan model.

Stefan number of the solid c_s(T_m − T_i)/ℓ
far end of the solid in units of (α_l t_r)^(1/2)

assumptions.text: Pure conduction in both phases with constant properties, and one density for both phases (no flow from the change of density).
A sharp front at the melting temperature, without supercooling and without a mushy zone.
A half-space: the far end x_f of the solid is far beyond the thermal layer, X_f ≫ 2λ/ν + 8√κ·1, so the similarity solution with x_f → ∞ applies.
Ste_s = 0 (T_i = T_m) gives the one-phase model of Font, whose group β = ℓ/(c(T_f − T_c)) is the reciprocal of the Stefan number used here.

symbolic: The exact groups Ste_l, Ste_s and κ = α_s/α_l in rationals, and the exact reduction of the Stefan condition to the dimensionless form with the factor Ste_l.
The similarity reduction η = x/(2(α_l t)^(1/2)): the erf profiles satisfy the heat equation and both front conditions, and the front condition gives the transcendental equation for λ.
numerical: λ by bisection on the decreasing function F(λ) to the last bit; erf and erfc to about 1e-15.
The latent-energy balance by Simpson quadrature of the profiles, against the closed-form energy input.

An independent transient solution: a front-fixing finite-difference scheme in both phases (backward Euler, central differences), started from a profile that is not the similarity profile, on three meshes.

dominant-balance.reason: The latent heat and the sensible heat compete in the front condition. For Ste_l ≪ 1 the latent heat controls and the liquid profile is nearly linear (quasi-steady); for Ste_l ≫ 1 the sensible heat controls. Ste_s and κ measure how much heat the cold solid takes from the front.

asymptotic.reason: The one-phase small-Stefan limit gives λ² = Ste_l/2 − Ste_l²/6 + O(Ste_l³), the quasi-steady front s² = 2Ste_l α_l t at first order. The page compares it with the exact root.

stability.reason: The declared model is the melting problem with a stable planar front. A supercooled liquid or a solidification front with constitutional supercooling can lose stability: that needs a separate declaration with a curved front.

bifurcation.reason: F(λ) decreases strictly from +∞ to −∞, so the similarity solution is unique for each Ste_l, Ste_s and κ. No branch exists to follow.

limitations: One density for both phases: a change of volume at melting needs a separate declaration with the flow it causes.
A half-space with a fixed wall temperature: a finite slab, a convective wall or a heat flux at the wall breaks the similarity and needs a numerical declaration.
Pure conduction: natural convection in the melt needs a separate declaration.

acceptance.reference: Neumann's similarity solution: Roscani and Tarzia, eqs. (3.28) to (3.31) with fractional order 1; with Ste_s = 0 Font's eq. (8), βπ^(1/2)λ erf(λ)e^(λ²) = 1 with β = 1/Ste_l. An independent root from mpmath (tools/family_references.py).
acceptance.tolerance: Exact for the groups; λ within 1e-12 of mpmath; the latent-energy balance within 1e-9; the transient front within 1e-3 relative on the finest mesh, with second-order convergence.
checks: λ is the root of the transcendental equation and agrees with mpmath.
The energy that enters through the wall equals the latent heat of the melted layer plus the sensible heat of both phases.
An independent transient solution moves the front as s = 2λ(α_l t)^(1/2).

solver.method: Bisection for λ; closed-form similarity profiles; Simpson quadrature for the energy balance; front-fixing finite differences (backward Euler) for the transient check.
solver.discretization: Transient check: 20, 40 and 80 intervals in the liquid and twice as many in the solid, with 2 000, 4 000 and 8 000 steps geometric in time from τ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ to 1/4 in units of t with X = 2(α_l t)^(1/2).
solver.convergence: The front error falls by about 4 for each halving of the mesh (second order in space); the finest error is the stated tolerance.
solver.reproducibility: IEEE double precision; no random numbers. The reference script tools/family_references.py pins mpmath.

correlation.name: Rohsenow's nucleate pool-boiling correlation (1952)
correlation.data: Rohsenow compared the correlation with data for water boiling on a 0.61 mm platinum wire from 1 atm to 167.7 atm (Fig. 9.7). Typical errors are 100 % in q and 25 % in ΔT_e (section 9.2).

peak.name: Peak heat flux on a large flat heater (Lienhard and Dhir)

zuber.text: The Zuber–Kutateladze constant π/24 ≈ 0.131 is 14 % lower. Lienhard and Lienhard state that eqn. (9.12) cannot be applied directly to any actual heater.

peak.conditions: Horizontal flat plates with side walls, no entrained side flow, a well-wetted surface, and a heater larger than about 3λ_d1 (section 9.3).

boiling.otherFluids: Table 9.2 also lists CCl₄, benzene, n-pentane, ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol, n-butyl alcohol and K₂CO₃ solutions, all with s = 1.7. They need a declaration of their own.

pressure.text: Rohsenow's data for water span 1 atm to 167.7 atm.

range.text: The data of Fig. 9.7 lie between c_pΔT_e/(h_fg Pr) ≈ 0.006 and 0.06.

range.data: The page reads the data range of Rohsenow's comparison from Fig. 9.7 as 0.006 ≤ c_pΔT_e/(h_fg Pr) ≤ 0.06.

regions.label: Below the data: natural convection or isolated bubbles; the page refuses the correlation
Inside the data of Rohsenow's comparison
Above the data; the page refuses the correlation

regime.data: Nucleate boiling ends at the peak heat flux q_max of eqn. (9.11).

regions.label: Nucleate boiling: below the peak heat flux
Beyond the peak heat flux: transition or film boiling needs a separate declaration

correction.text: Sadasivan and Lienhard's latent-heat correction for Pr ≥ 0.6.

state.data: Re_c = Γ_c/μ. Ripples appear at Re_c ≈ 7 and raise h by up to about 20 % before the laminar–turbulent transition at Re_c ≈ 400 (data of Gregorig, Kern and Turek for water). Many American texts use 4Γ_c/μ instead.

regions.label: Wave-free laminar film: Nusselt's theory agrees with the data
Rippled laminar film: the data lie up to about 20 % above Nusselt's theory
Turbulent film: the declared model does not apply
